summary: The article provides a generally accurate overview of SEBI's reintroduction of open-market buybacks and their tax implications, though some tax rates and exemption limits are outdated.

claims.claim: SEBI has reintroduced open-market share buybacks, effective August 1, 2026, allowing companies to repurchase their shares via stock exchanges.
claims.note: SEBI has indeed reintroduced open-market share buybacks effective August 1, 2026.

claims.claim: When a company buys back shares through a tender offer, the company itself pays a tax (previously Dividend Distribution Tax, now a specific tax under Section 115QA of the Income Tax Act) on the amount paid to shareholders.
claims.note: Budget 2025 shifted the tax burden on buybacks from the company to the shareholders, treating it as dividend income. Section 115QA previously applied to the company, but its regime has been eliminated for buybacks after October 1, 2024.

claims.claim: For investors, the gains from tender offer buybacks are exempt from tax in their hands, as the company is liable to pay tax under Section 115QA of the Income Tax Act, 1961.
claims.note: As per Budget 2025, the tax burden on buybacks has shifted to shareholders, and the proceeds are treated as dividend income, taxable in the hands of the shareholder, not exempt. The company is no longer liable to pay tax under Section 115QA for buybacks after October 1, 2024.

claims.claim: If you sell shares within 12 months of acquiring them, any profit you make is considered a Short-Term Capital Gain (STCG). This STCG is added to your total income and taxed at your applicable income tax slab rate. For instance, if you are in the 30% tax bracket, your STCG will be taxed at 30% (plus surcharge and cess, if applicable).
claims.note: For listed equity shares where STT is paid, STCG is taxed at a flat rate of 20% under Section 111A, not at the individual's slab rate. This rate was increased from 15% in Budget 2024, effective July 23, 2024.

claims.claim: If you sell shares after holding them for more than 12 months, any profit is considered a Long-Term Capital Gain (LTCG). Under current income tax laws (Section 112A of the Income Tax Act, 1961), LTCG from the sale of equity shares listed on a recognised stock exchange is taxed at a concessional rate. The first ₹1 lakh of LTCG in a financial year is exempt from tax. Any LTCG exceeding ₹1 lakh is taxed at a flat rate of 10% (plus surcharge and cess, if applicable), without the benefit of indexation.
claims.note: As per Budget 2024, effective July 23, 2024, the LTCG tax rate on listed equity shares under Section 112A has been increased to 12.5%, and the exemption limit has been raised to ₹1.25 lakh. The article states 10% and ₹1 lakh respectively.

claims.claim: It's important to note that the Securities Transaction Tax (STT) would have already been paid at the time of purchase and sale of these shares on the stock exchange, which is a prerequisite for availing the concessional LTCG tax rate.
claims.note: Payment of STT on both acquisition and sale of listed equity shares is a prerequisite for the concessional LTCG tax rate under Section 112A.

claims.claim: The first ₹1,00,000 of LTCG in a financial year is exempt.
claims.note: The LTCG exemption limit for listed equity shares under Section 112A was increased to ₹1.25 lakh in Budget 2024, effective July 23, 2024.

claims.claim: LTCG Tax Rate: 10% (under Section 112A of the Income Tax Act, 1961).
claims.note: The LTCG tax rate under Section 112A for listed equity shares was increased to 12.5% in Budget 2024, effective July 23, 2024.

article_title: Open-Market Buybacks: Taxing Your Gains and Investor Strategy
